intro: The third movement of the Symphony No. 5, Op. 67, opens in the cellos and double basses, followed by a horn call. When the scherzo returns, the horn call is played softly, and the timpani then begin the long passage that leads into the finale.

sections.label: A · Low strings and horn calls
sections.mNote: Low C-minor arpeggios, then horn calls on repeated notes

sections.label: B · Fugue in the basses, C major
sections.mNote: Running quavers climb through the strings in C major.

sections.label: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
sections.mNote: The horn rhythm returns in clarinets, bassoons and plucked strings.

sections.label: Link · Timpani beneath held strings
sections.mNote: Repeated C leads into the finale without a break.

cues.title: Low strings, C minor arpeggios
cues.text: Cellos and double basses climb through the notes of C minor. A quiet reply comes from the orchestra above, followed by a fermata. The low strings play the phrase again, and the three-beat metre stays suspended between these phrases.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5, printed p. 37: low-string arpeggios, orchestral replies and fermatas. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0c/IMSLP52624-PMLP01586-Beethoven_Werke_Breitkopf_Serie_1_No_5_Op_67.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horn entry, opening rhythm
cues.text: After the cellos climb through a chord, the horns enter with the rhythm that opened the symphony, three short notes followed by a long one. They repeat a single pitch.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 37–38. The rhythmic connection is discussed by Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trio in C major, cellos and basses
cues.text: The trio is in C major. Cellos and double basses play a running tune, and the other strings take it up in turn, each entering before the previous entry has finished.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 42–46: C-major trio and imitative string entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sketches and Mozart’s G minor Symphony
cues.text: Beethoven’s sketches show that the first and third movements were conceived first. In the sketchbook he used for the Eroica, this scherzo is linked to the finale of Mozart’s G minor Symphony, which also begins by climbing a minor triad.
cues.evidence: Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven’s Symphonies, pp. 97 and 100, as cited by the Eastman School of Music: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/. Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, IV, opening.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1808
cues.text: On 22 December 1808 Beethoven introduced the Fifth and Sixth symphonies in the same concert at the Theater an der Wien. He also played his Fourth Piano Concerto. The evening included music from the Mass in C and ended with the Choral Fantasy.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, Symphony No. 5, première details and concert programme: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: Repeat of scherzo and trio
cues.text: Beethoven’s autograph has the scherzo and trio played twice before the last scherzo. The first printed parts leave the repeat out, and Jonathan Del Mar’s Bärenreiter edition argues that Beethoven himself ordered the cut. This performance plays the shorter form.
cues.evidence: Jonathan Del Mar, “New Urtext Edition: Beethoven Symphonies 1–9”, British Academy: duplicate first-performance parts copied from the lost engraver’s copy include the written-out repeat, and the pages containing it were excised, which he judges could only have been done on Beethoven’s own instructions. https://www.thebritishacademy.ac.uk/documents/551/24-delmar.pdf. The three-part form of the first published parts of 1809: Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: Return of the scherzo, pianissimo
cues.text: The opening returns in C minor, rewritten and pianissimo. Clarinets and bassoons exchange the repeated-note rhythm with pizzicato strings.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 46–49: rewritten scherzo return, pianissimo winds and pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Instruments held back for the finale
cues.text: The piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones do not play in this movement. Beethoven gave them their first notes in the finale.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score: piccolo, contrabassoon and three trombones first appear in movement IV. Instrumentation also listed at https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Transition to the finale
cues.text: The timpani repeat C. Cellos and basses hold A♭ beneath C in the first violins and violas. The violins begin to move, and a long crescendo leads without a break into the C major finale.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 50–52: A♭ in the low strings, C in first violins, violas and timpani, followed by the crescendo and uninterrupted finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Scherzo into the C-major trio
transitions.from: A · Low strings and horn calls
transitions.to: B · Fugue in the basses, C major
transitions.how: The scherzo closes in C minor. The trio turns to C major, and the cellos and double basses open it in running quavers. The tune passes upwards through successive imitative string entries, and the bassoons join them. The metre remains in three beats to the bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 42–46: C-major trio and successive imitative entries.

transitions.title: Trio to quiet scherzo reprise
transitions.from: B · Fugue in the basses, C major
transitions.to: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
transitions.how: The trio dies down, and the low-string arpeggio returns in C minor. The scherzo comes back quietly. The repeated-note call moves to clarinets and bassoons, with pizzicato strings around it, so the rhythm is now played in short, dry attacks (Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 45–49).
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 45–49: diminishing trio and rescored scherzo return.

transitions.title: Timpani under held strings
transitions.from: A′ · Plucked strings and quiet winds
transitions.how: The detached phrases stop. Cellos and basses hold A♭; first violins and violas hold C, marked pianississimo. The timpani repeat C against that bass. The violin line gradually begins to move, and the orchestra builds a crescendo that carries the chord into the finale’s C major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed pp. 50–52. The pedal C is in the timpani; the string bass begins on A♭.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, III, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 37–51: low-string opening, horn calls, C-major fugato, plucked return and timpani bridge into the finale.

timeline.note: Cellos and double basses begin the quiet rising arpeggio in C minor.
Quiet violin phrases answer the low strings, with winds and horns beneath them.
The horns play their repeated-note call above the strings.
Winds, brass and timpani join the strings in the scherzo’s forceful closing phrases.
Cellos and basses play the quick C-major fugue subject.
Violas, violins and bassoons join the running subject in successive entries.
Woodwinds punctuate the strings’ overlapping phrases.
The opening low-string arpeggio returns quietly, before the plucked continuation.
Quiet woodwinds trade the repeated notes with plucked and lightly bowed strings.
The timpani repeat C against the A♭ held by cellos and basses.
The violin line rises above held lower strings and the timpani’s repeated C.
Woodwinds, horns and trumpets join the crescendo towards the finale.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
